note: The lab's public register of research leads. Edit this file, then run tools/leads/render_leads.py and tools/leads/check_leads.py. Fields and rules: leads/README.md. Nothing private goes here.

leads.title: Unsorted remainder of the trial atlas, sorted by a local model with exact-quote checks
leads.question: Can a local model propose a class for the primary outcomes the atlas lexicon leaves unsorted, with every proposal backed by an exact quote from the registry record?
leads.why_it_matters: Without it, a large unsorted remainder would hide part of what CF trials register as their main outcome.

sources.ref: trial atlas route, first real runs (board T-0130)
sources.note: Done in the atlas route; the tools are in pull request cf-research#39. A verified quote proves only that the words exist in the record.

guard.note: Counts are computed from the snapshot; any registry text shown is quoted verbatim and checked against the record.

must_not_claim: That a model's class for an outcome is correct because its quote was found in the record.
That the atlas classes measure trial quality.

leads.title: Results posted, and registry records linked to publications by exact trial-id match
leads.question: For CF trials in the registry, how many have results posted, and how many have a publication that cites their trial id exactly?
leads.why_it_matters: Researchers and clinicians weigh evidence differently when they know how much of the registered trial record reached results or a paper.

sources.ref: a published study of registry-to-publication links found in the 2026-10-10 literature search; citation to be recorded
sources.note: Agent-read abstract, not re-read here: about 23.2 percent of trials had a direct registry-to-PubMed link and about 44 percent of the apparently unlinked had a paper when searched by hand. Both figures are T0.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Suggested as a follow-on view.

fields_missing: publication links by trial id (Europe PMC or PubMed search)

guard.note: An exact trial-id match gives a lower bound only, and every count says so in the same sentence.

must_not_claim: That a trial without a matched paper is unpublished.
That a match rate measures a sponsor's conduct.

leads.title: How differently trials define pulmonary exacerbation, FEV1 and sweat chloride outcomes
leads.question: How many distinct definitions do CF trials register for pulmonary exacerbation, FEV1 and sweat chloride outcomes, counted by rule facets such as time frame and threshold?
leads.why_it_matters: Outcomes defined in different ways are hard to compare across trials, and a count of the definitions shows where comparison needs care.

sources.ref: a systematic review of outcomes in 144 CF studies, found in the 2026-10-10 literature search; citation to be recorded
sources.note: Agent-read abstract: it reported "a wide range of outcomes and corresponding endpoints".

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10

guard.note: Counts of definitions by facet are computed; a definition shown is the registry text, quoted verbatim.

must_not_claim: That one definition is better or worse than another.
That heterogeneity means a trial was badly designed.

leads.title: Registered outcomes before and after CFTR modulator approvals
leads.question: Did the mix of registered primary outcomes in CF trials shift between the eras around each modulator approval?
leads.why_it_matters: Trial designers and clinicians may want to see how registered endpoints changed as modulators changed care.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Start dates with no date type are shown as a band, not placed in an era.

fields_missing: US approval dates from openFDA Drugs@FDA

guard.note: Era counts are computed; approval dates come from openFDA records; the framing is labelled a lab position.

must_not_claim: That an approval caused any change in what trials register (no causal words).
That a start date with no date type belongs to a particular era.

leads.title: Embeddings and seeded clustering as an internal aid for finding lexicon terms
leads.question: Can embeddings with clusters seeded by the existing lexicon classes surface outcome wording the lexicon misses?
leads.why_it_matters: A better lexicon sorts more outcomes by rule, so fewer depend on a model's proposal.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: A local embedding model is not yet onboarded; it would go through the model-onboarding checklist first.

guard.note: Internal only: a cluster suggests terms for a person to add as rules; clusters never publish.

must_not_claim: That a cluster is a category of outcome.
Any count or figure from clusters.

leads.title: Map atlas classes to a published outcome taxonomy
leads.question: Can each atlas class be placed under a domain of the Dodd et al. 2018 outcome taxonomy, and which classes fit none?
leads.why_it_matters: A shared taxonomy lets others compare the atlas with outcome work in other conditions.

sources.ref: Dodd et al. 2018, a taxonomy of outcome domains, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5854263/
sources.note: The controlling agent read the abstract page text: 38 outcome domains in five core areas; it says registry outcomes "can be entered as free text only".

sources.ref: a report that mapping outcome concepts to UMLS covered only part of them, found in the 2026-10-10 literature search; citation to be recorded
sources.note: Agent-read: about 44 percent of outcome concepts covered. T0 here.

fields_missing: the taxonomy's domain list, read from the open-access article

guard.note: Domain names come from the open-access article under its licence; each mapping is a lab position until a person reviews it.

must_not_claim: That the mapping is endorsed by the taxonomy's authors.
That a class that fits no domain is a gap in CF research.

leads.title: Trials per class, deduplicated by lead sponsor
leads.question: How many distinct lead sponsors register trials in each atlas class, once spelling variants of one sponsor are merged by an alias table?
leads.why_it_matters: A sponsor count shows whether a class rests on many groups or a few, without ranking anyone.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: The reviews advised against a network graph, which reads as a ranking.

fields_missing: an alias table for sponsor names (lab-made)

guard.note: Counts are computed; sponsor names are as the registry records them, and every alias merge is listed.

must_not_claim: A ranking of sponsors or any judgement of a sponsor.
That a sponsor's count reflects its contribution to CF care.

leads.title: Registered outcome time frame compared with registered start and completion dates
leads.question: How often does a primary outcome's registered time frame fit inside the span between the registered start and completion dates?
leads.why_it_matters: A mismatch flags records a reader should check before relying on the time frame.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Completion dates are not in the first snapshot.

guard.note: Comparisons are computed from registry fields; time frames shown are quoted verbatim.

must_not_claim: That a mismatch is an error by the sponsor.
That a record is wrong; it may be planned or estimated.
leads.notes: Needs a re-fetch with more fields; the maintainer approves any new fetch.

leads.title: Stopped trials and the reasons sponsors wrote
leads.question: For CF trials recorded as stopped, what reasons did the sponsors write, grouped without rewording?
leads.why_it_matters: Reasons for stopping help trial designers plan recruitment and feasibility.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: The why-stopped field is not in the first snapshot.

guard.note: Reasons are shown as the sponsor wrote them; group counts are computed.

must_not_claim: That a trial stopped for safety or efficacy unless its record says so.
Any reason the sponsor did not write.
leads.notes: Needs a re-fetch with more fields; the maintainer approves any new fetch.

leads.title: Age bands trials admit, beside the age mix registries report
leads.question: Which age bands do CF trials admit, and how does that compare with the age groups registry reports describe?
leads.why_it_matters: Clinicians and families may want to see which age groups are less often admitted to trials.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Minimum and maximum age are not in the first snapshot.

guard.note: Trial counts are computed; registry age figures are quoted verbatim with the report and page, read with the registry reading guides.

must_not_claim: Counts of patients from trial records; the trial side counts trials only.
Any comparison of one registry's figures with another's.
That a person of a given age can or cannot join a trial.

leads.title: Crosswalk between registry measures and trial outcomes
leads.question: Which outcomes that trials register correspond to measures that patient registries report?
leads.why_it_matters: A crosswalk would show where trial outcomes and routine registry data speak the same language.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10

fields_missing: registry measure definitions, read from the reports

guard.note: Each match is a lab position that a person labels; definitions on both sides are quoted verbatim.

must_not_claim: That a trial outcome and a registry measure are the same thing because their names match.
Any match a person has not labelled.

leads.title: Atlas classes beside the CF core outcome set effort and frequent primary outcomes
leads.question: How do the atlas classes line up with the CF core outcome set work listed in the COMET database, and with methods that find frequent primary outcomes by text mining?
leads.why_it_matters: A core outcome set is what trialists may be asked to measure, so alignment with it makes the atlas useful to them.

sources.ref: COMET database, study 882 (a CF core outcome set effort)
sources.note: Agent-read: status ongoing at the time read; check the current status before any use.

sources.ref: a 2021 MEDINFO paper on frequent primary outcomes by text mining, found in the 2026-10-10 literature search; citation to be recorded
sources.note: Agent-read: it covered 5,090 trials. T0.

fields_missing: the core outcome set's outcome list, when published

guard.note: Outcome names from a core outcome set are quoted from its open-access publication; any alignment is a lab position.

must_not_claim: A CF core outcome set that has not been published.
That the atlas proposes or endorses a core outcome set.
That frequency of use makes an outcome a good one.

leads.title: How often primary outcomes change over a record's history
leads.question: How often is a CF trial's registered primary outcome changed after the trial starts?
leads.why_it_matters: Outcome changes after a trial starts are something readers of results want to know about.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: An idea only; record history is not in the catalog.

not_in_catalog: ClinicalTrials.gov record history (versions of a record)

guard.note: Change counts would be computed from versions; any changed text is quoted verbatim.

must_not_claim: That a change was improper; many changes are corrections or planned updates.
Anything about a named trial or sponsor.
leads.notes: Needs a catalog entry, with its terms read, before any data is touched.

leads.title: AACT for comparing CF trials with all registered trials
leads.question: Could AACT, a relational copy of ClinicalTrials.gov, give the denominators to compare CF trials with all trials?
leads.why_it_matters: A comparison with all trials tells whether a CF pattern is particular to CF or common to trials generally.

sources.ref: three blind council reviews of the atlas, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Its terms need checking before any use.

guard.note: Only computed counts with the snapshot date; nothing until the catalog records what AACT permits.

must_not_claim: That CF trials are better or worse than other trials.
Any figure from AACT before its terms are recorded in the catalog.

leads.title: Start dates with no recorded date type in older records
leads.question: What else do older registry records lack, beyond the start date type observed missing on the first run?
leads.why_it_matters: Readers of any trend over time need to know which years rest on less complete records.

sources.ref: trial atlas, first real run, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Observed: a start date with no type in a large share of in-scope records, all with start years before 2018. Not re-counted here.

sources.ref: NLM Technical Bulletin item on older ClinicalTrials.gov records; link to be recorded
sources.note: It says older records "may be missing information". Our inference about the cause is T0.

guard.note: The share is computed from the snapshot; the bulletin is quoted verbatim; the cause stays an inference.

must_not_claim: Why older records lack the date type, beyond what the registry states.
That records without a date type are wrong.
leads.notes: A data-quality note for the atlas, and a question about the other fields.

leads.title: A measured, quote-verified classifier for registry primary outcomes
leads.question: How well does the atlas's quote-verified classifier agree with a frozen, person-labelled set of primary outcomes?
leads.why_it_matters: A published agreement measure would let other groups judge whether such a classifier is fit for their own use.

sources.ref: a quick literature search, 2026-10-10
sources.note: No published evaluation of a registry primary-outcome classifier with agreement numbers was found; an empty search is not proof of absence.

sources.ref: trial atlas, first real run, blind challenger, 2026-10-10
sources.note: The challenger agreed on 84 percent of 150 sampled entries (95 percent interval 77 to 89); agreement is not correctness.

guard.note: A methods note only after the frozen set is measured; all agreement figures are computed with their intervals.

must_not_claim: That the classifier is accurate on the strength of model-to-model agreement.
That no such classifier has been published.

leads.title: Spanish (es-MX) outcome terms grounded in Spanish open-access sources
leads.question: Which Spanish-language open-access sources could ground Mexican Spanish names for the atlas classes?
leads.why_it_matters: Spanish-speaking families and clinicians deserve terms that come from Spanish sources, not from a model's translation.

sources.ref: Europe PMC search during the atlas work, 2026-10-10
sources.note: Europe PMC returned thin Spanish full text.

guard.note: A term is used only with a Spanish open-access source whose licence allows it; otherwise it is a lab position the maintainer reviews.

must_not_claim: That a Spanish term is standard or official without a source that says so.
A machine translation presented as a sourced term.

leads.title: Single-use outcome instruments as a long tail
leads.question: How many outcome instruments in CF trials appear in only one trial, shown as an 'other or single-use instrument' view?
leads.why_it_matters: A long tail of single-use instruments makes results hard to pool, and a count shows its size.

sources.ref: a preprint review of gastrointestinal outcomes in CF, found in the 2026-10-10 literature search; citation to be recorded
sources.note: Agent-read preprint abstract: 172 of 246 instruments were used in only one study. T0.

guard.note: Counts are computed; instrument names are shown as registered.

must_not_claim: That a single-use instrument is invalid or poor.
The preprint's figures as established; they are T0 here.

leads.title: Topics raised at a conference, worth checking in the literature
leads.question: Which topics raised at a conference have published, open-access evidence we can read and cite?
leads.why_it_matters: Conference topics can point to questions researchers are working on now.

sources.ref: private

guard.note: Only published, open-access sources are cited; nothing from the conference itself is repeated.

must_not_claim: Anything a presenter said or showed, or who presented it.
That a topic is established before a published source is read.
leads.notes: Details are kept in the maintainer's private folder, not here.
